newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan sees S.Africa trade growing 10 pct a year.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan sees S.Africa trade growing 10 pct a year.

text.p: Taiwan Vice-Premier Hsu Li-teh, cementing ties with the island's biggest diplomatic ally, said bilateral trade with South Africa would grow 10 percent a year, the state Central News Agency reported on Wednesday.

"There is still a lot of room for bilateral trade to grow and if the two sides cooperate, I believe the amount of bilateral trade will grow 10 percent annually," Hsu was quoted as saying in South Africa.
Taipei-Pretoria trade totalled US$1.871 billion in 1995.
Pretoria is the biggest of Taipei's 30 diplomatic allies but has publicly expressed its desire for ties with Beijing, which demands it sever diplomatic relations with Taiwan first.
China has regarded Taiwan as a renegade province not entitled to foreign ties since a civil war split them in 1949.
Since Hsu's nine-day visit began on August 25, Taiwan has said it would sign contracts to build a US$3 billion to $5 billion petrochemical zone in the republic.
"The main purpose of the visit is to invest in South Africa, not only in petrochemicals but also in the manufacturing, steel and telecommunication industries," Hsu was quoted as saying.
"The most we want is to set up an industrial park (in South Africa) to attract labour-intensive Taiwanese businesses that want to move abroad," he said.
Taiwan said on Wednesday it had begun initial discussions with Pretoria on sales of Taiwan's home-grown AT-3 trainer jets.

The island's diplomatic isolation has intensified since 1971, when Beijing took China's United Nations seat from Taipei, but Taiwan keeps close economic ties with many countries with its huge market clout.

Yet South African trade ties with China have soared in recent years. Its exports to China doubled in 1995 to one billion rand ($231 million) -- less than half of its exports to Taiwan, which grew to 2.5 billion rand ($577 million).
President Nelson Mandela told Hsu on Monday that South Africa would stand by Taiwan's exiled Republic of China government but also wanted to improve relations with China.
Some 278 Taiwan businesses have operations in South Africa with investments totalling $1.5 billion, according to Taiwan figures.
